name: Yamanba / manba makeup

card.summary: An exaggerated Japanese gyaru look with a very deep tan, bleached or neon hair and white eye and lip makeup, used to look strikingly bold and different from conventional beauty.
card.note: Deep tanning carries UV skin risks.

quick.overview:
Yamanba, also shortened to manba, is a more extreme offshoot of the ganguro fashion that began in 1990s Japan. The look centres on a deep tan, white lipstick and pastel or white eye makeup, often with pale or neon hair, face gems and bright clothes.

It rejects the traditional ideal of pale skin and dark hair, and uses makeup to make the face stand out. It is named after the mountain witch of Japanese folklore, Yama-uba.
quick.how: Followers build the look with a dark tan (from tanning or dark foundation), white concealer on eyes and lips, pastel eyeshadow, bleached or colourful hair and extensions, circle lenses and accessories. Early versions used glitter stickers under the eyes.
quick.risks: The main health concern is UV exposure from deep tanning, a general skin-health consideration for any deliberate tanning. Bleaching hair can cause breakage. Social attention and press criticism were part of the style's history.

lead: Yamanba (also manba) is an extreme form of ganguro, a Japanese youth fashion from the mid-1990s that grew out of gyaru culture around Tokyo's Shibuya and Ikebukuro. It is named after Yama-uba, a mountain witch of Japanese folklore. [1]

Followers use makeup and styling to achieve a bold, stylised appearance: a deep tan, white lipstick, pastel or white eye makeup, bright or bleached hair, coloured circle lenses and accessories such as leis. [1]

chain: Deep tan and pale white eye and lip makeup
Striking look that rejects the pale-skin ideal
angle.text: Makeup creates the signature contrast: white concealer used as lipstick and eyeshadow against a dark tan, with face gems or stickers. It is a style choice made to look dramatic rather than to match conventional beauty norms.

infobox: Deep tan, white lip and eye makeup, bleached or neon hair

paras: Ganguro began in the mid-1990s and peaked in the late 1990s, rejecting the traditional ideal of pale skin and dark hair. It faded around 2000 as a bihaku (light skin) craze emerged. Yamanba was the more extreme offshoot; as its popularity waned it grew bolder, with neon pink hair, dreadlock-like extensions and darker tans. By 2008 facial stickers had disappeared and leis were less common. The male counterpart is called Sentaa Guy, after Shibuya's Center Gai. [1]
Early yamanba looks included a deep tan, white lipstick, pastel eye makeup, metallic or glitter adhesives under the eyes, coloured circle lenses and Hawaiian leis. [1]

timeline.event: Ganguro begins in Shibuya and Ikebukuro. [1]
Bihaku light-skin trend rises as ganguro fades. [1]
Facial stickers have disappeared from the style. [1]
